name: Observability
summary: Logs, metrics and traces that tell you what your system is doing.
howItWorks: Observability means emitting enough telemetry to answer questions about production you didn’t think to ask in advance. Logs are timestamped records of events. Metrics are numbers aggregated over time, like requests per second or p95 latency. Traces follow one request across every service it touches. A collector such as OpenTelemetry gathers all three and ships them to storage, dashboards and alerting.
analogy: A car’s gauges, trip log and dashcam. The gauges show how it’s doing now, the log shows what happened, and the dashcam shows one whole journey.
useWhen: Every production system, from the first day
Alerting on symptoms users feel: errors, latency, saturation
Finding the slow step in a request that crosses many services
avoidWhen: Debug-level logging of everything in production; the bill grows fast
Alerting on every metric; page people only for what needs a human
example: A jump in p95 latency fires an alert. The trace of one slow request shows 1.8 s inside a single database query, and that service’s logs show the slowdown began right after a deploy.

providers.aws: CloudWatch (metrics, Logs, Application Signals; X-Ray traces in the CloudWatch console)
providers.oss: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger, GreptimeDB, ClickStack (ClickHouse with the HyperDX UI and an OpenTelemetry collector); agents: Fluentd, Fluent Bit, Logstash, Telegraf, Vector; hosted: Datadog, Better Stack, Sentry (errors and traces)

diagram.caption: Two services emit logs, metrics and traces. The collector routes each kind to its own store, and now and then a metric crosses its threshold and fires an alert.

story: The word comes from control theory: in 1960 Rudolf Kálmán described a system as observable if its internal state can be inferred from its outputs. Running software started with simpler questions. Nagios, first released as NetSaint in 1999, ran checks against hosts and services and sent an alert when something failed and again when it recovered. Graphite, and StatsD, which Etsy released in early 2011, let engineers send and chart almost any number they cared about.

Distributed systems outgrew that. Google’s 2010 Dapper paper described how one request could touch many services, written by different teams in different languages across thousands of machines, and how sampling made it cheap enough to trace requests in production. In 2012 SoundCloud, with hundreds of services and thousands of instances, started Prometheus because its StatsD and Graphite setup couldn’t slice metrics by instance or endpoint.

“Observability” became the name for the goal: being able to answer questions about production you didn’t think to ask in advance, rather than only watching checks and dashboards someone set up beforehand. Metrics, logs and traces became known as its three pillars. In 2019 the OpenTracing and OpenCensus projects merged into OpenTelemetry, a vendor-neutral way to produce all three, which graduated from the CNCF in May 2026.

choices.why: When one user action crosses dozens of services, per-host graphs can show that something is slow but not where. A trace records each step of one request, with timings, so the slow hop stands out.
Dapper’s designers needed tracing to be always on with low overhead, so they recorded only a fraction of requests. Sampling is still how tracing stays affordable at scale.
Labels such as instance, endpoint and status let you slice the same data in ways nobody planned for, which is the difference between monitoring known failures and exploring new ones.
Instrumenting code is the expensive part. A vendor-neutral standard means you instrument once and can change where the data goes without touching application code.

timeline.text: Rudolf Kálmán defines observability in control theory
NetSaint, later renamed Nagios, is released
Google publishes the Dapper paper on distributed tracing
OpenTracing and OpenCensus merge into OpenTelemetry
OpenTelemetry graduates from the CNCF in May
